q: Who is the author of the chapter "Netaji ka Chashma"?
e: Swayam Prakash is the author of the story "Netaji ka Chashma".

q: In which prose genre is the lesson "Netaji ka Chashma" written?
e: "Netaji ka Chashma" is a sensitive and satirical short story.

q: Which great leader's statue was installed at the main intersection of the town?
e: The statue of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose was installed at the main square of the town market.

q: What material was Netaji's statue made of?
e: The statue of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose was made of marble stone.

q: Approximately how tall was Netaji's statue?
e: Netaji's bust was about two feet tall from the tip of the cap to the second button of the coat.

q: After how many days did Haldar Sahab pass through that town for company work?
e: Haldar Sahab had to pass through that town every fifteenth day for his company work.

q: Who used to change the spectacles on Netaji's statue?
e: Captain Chashmewala used to change the real spectacles on Netaji's statue.

q: What was the name of the sculptor who made Netaji's statue?
e: Master Motilal, the drawing teacher of the town's only high school, made Netaji's statue.

q: Which subject did Master Motilal teach in school?
e: Master Motilal was the only drawing teacher at the town's high school.

q: In what attire was Netaji's statue sculpted?
e: Netaji's statue was in military uniform, reminding viewers of slogans like "Dilli Chalo".

q: What did Haldar Sahab eat whenever he stopped in the town?
e: Haldar Sahab always stopped at the intersection to eat paan from the panwala's shop.

q: What kind of person was the panwala in "Netaji ka Chashma"?
e: The panwala himself was a dark, fat, and jolly man whose belly jiggled when he laughed.

q: What work did Captain Chashmewala do?
e: Captain was a hawker who sold spectacles from street to street hung on a bamboo pole.

q: What kind of spectacles was on Netaji's statue at the end of the story?
e: After Captain's death, a child eventually placed a small spectacle made of reed (sarkanda) on the statue.

q: Which small factory was located in the town?
e: The opening description of the lesson mentions that the town had a small cement factory.

q: How many open-air cinema halls were there in the town?
e: There were two open-air cinema halls in the town.

q: In how much time did the sculptor promise to finish and deliver Netaji's statue?
e: Master Motilal assured the town municipality that he would complete and deliver the statue within a month.

q: What was the one shortcoming left in Master Motilal's statue?
o: There was no cap on the statue
There were no spectacles on the statue's eyes
The colour of the statue was faded
e: The marble statue was complete, except there were no stone spectacles on Netaji's eyes.

q: How did the spectacles appear to Haldar Sahab when he first saw the statue?
e: The statue was made of marble, but a wide black frame of real spectacles was put on it.

q: What kind of smile spread across Haldar Sahab's face when he first saw real spectacles on the statue?
e: Seeing a stone statue with real spectacles, an amused and curious smile spread across Haldar Sahab's face.

q: What did Captain Chashmewala wear on his head?
e: Captain was a very old, frail, lame man who wore a Gandhi cap on his head and dark glasses on his eyes.

q: What did Captain carry in one of his hands?
e: Captain carried a small box in one hand and many spectacles hung on a bamboo pole in the other.

q: Who called Captain "mad" according to the story?
e: Mocking Captain, the panwala said, "What will that lame man do in the army! He is mad, mad!"

q: Who gave Haldar Sahab the news of Captain's death?
e: When no spectacles appeared on the statue, upon asking, the panwala sadly told him, "Sahab, Captain died."

q: Which slogans came to mind upon looking at Netaji's statue?
o: Dilli Chalo and Tum Mujhe Khoon Do
e: Looking at Netaji's statue in military uniform, slogans like "Dilli Chalo" and "Tum Mujhe Khoon Do" came to mind.

q: Where was Swayam Prakash born?
e: Swayam Prakash was born in 1947 in Indore (Madhya Pradesh), though his childhood was spent in Rajasthan.

q: Which literary magazine was Swayam Prakash associated with as an editor?
e: While living in Bhopal, Swayam Prakash was associated with editing the magazine "Vasudha".

q: According to Haldar Sahab, whose effort was commendable regarding the town's statue?
o: The patriotic effort of the town's citizens
e: Haldar Sahab thought that overall, this effort by the citizens of the town was commendable because the spirit matters most.

q: How did the statue appear to Haldar Sahab at the square immediately after Captain's death?
e: After Captain died, when Haldar Sahab passed the square, there were no spectacles on the statue's eyes.

q: What was Haldar Sahab's emotional state upon seeing the reed spectacles at the end?
o: He became emotional and his eyes filled with tears
e: Haldar Sahab was deeply moved by this small gesture and his eyes welled up seeing patriotism alive in children.

q: Why must the municipality have assigned the statue-making job to the local drawing teacher?
o: Because he was a world-famous sculptor
Because he offered to work for free
Due to lack of information on good sculptors, low budget, and hurry as the tenure was ending
Because nobody else lived in the town
e: Due to low budget, haste before the board's tenure ended, and lack of knowledge about good sculptors, the work was given to the local drawing teacher.

q: What does "bust" mean, as used for Netaji's statue in the story?
e: A sculpture extending from the top of the head/cap down to the chest (second coat button) is called a bust.

q: Why did Captain Chashmewala keep changing the spectacles on Netaji's statue?
o: When a customer wanted the frame on the statue, he gave it to them and put another frame on the statue
He wanted to mock the statue
The municipality gave him a new frame daily
The spectacles used to blow away in the wind
e: If a customer liked the frame on the statue, Captain would apologize to Netaji, give that frame to the customer, and place another one on the statue.

q: What did Haldar Sahab ask the panwala that made him smile and say, "Captain Chashmewala"?
o: How do Netaji's spectacles change every time?
Which movie is playing in town?
Since when has the paan shop been open?
e: Seeing a different frame on the statue every time, Haldar Sahab asked the panwala how Netaji's spectacles kept changing.

q: Why did people call the spectacle-seller "Captain"?
o: Because he was a retired army captain
Because he was captain of a cricket team
Because of his deep respect for patriots, people called him Captain either out of respect or mockery
Because his real name was Captain Singh
e: He was neither in the army nor Netaji's comrade, yet people called him Captain owing to his patriotism and devotion to Netaji.

q: Which remark of the panwala about Captain made Haldar Sahab feel bad?
o: "What will that lame man do in the army? He is mad, mad!"
e: Haldar Sahab disliked the panwala mocking a patriot by saying, "What will that lame man do in the army? He is mad, mad!"

q: What did the narrator guess as possible reasons why Master Motilal did not carve the spectacles?
o: Carving transparent glass from stone was hard, or it broke while carving, or he forgot
He had gone out of town
e: According to the narrator, either Master forgot, or failed while trying to carve transparent stone glasses, or it broke/was skipped due to time.

q: Why is Haldar Sahab bewildered when he sees Captain for the first time?
o: Because Captain was a huge businessman
Because he expected a stout soldier, but saw an old, frail, lame hawker
e: Haldar Sahab imagined "Captain" as a soldier or INA veteran, but saw an old, frail hawker instead.

q: Why did Haldar Sahab avoid asking further questions about Captain?
o: Because his jeep driver ran away
Because he did not like the paan
Because the panwala was unwilling to talk further and the driver was getting restless
e: The panwala clearly showed unwillingness to discuss it further and the jeep driver was also getting restless.

q: After Captain's death, what fear began to haunt Haldar Sahab regarding the town?
o: That the paan shop would close
That the cement factory would shut down
That the statue would be demolished
That the statue would have no spectacles now and patriotism would vanish
e: Haldar Sahab feared that no one was left in the town to put spectacles on Netaji's spectacle-less statue.

q: What change was seen in the panwala's behaviour while telling about Captain's death?
o: He became sad and wiped his eyes with the corner of his dhoti
e: Even the panwala, who once mocked Captain, looked sad, bowed his head, and wiped his tears with his dhoti.

q: What did Haldar Sahab instruct his driver fifteen days later while passing through the town?
o: "Stop for longer at the square today"
"Do not stop at the square today, we will eat paan somewhere ahead"
"Park the car near the statue at the square"
e: Haldar Sahab did not want to see Netaji's statue without spectacles, so he told the driver not to stop at the square.

q: Despite ordering the driver not to stop, why did Haldar Sahab's eyes look toward the statue?
o: The panwala called out to him
A light was shining on the statue
e: Compelled by the habit of looking at the statue every time he passed, Haldar Sahab's eyes automatically turned toward it.

q: What did Haldar Sahab say to the driver upon seeing the reed spectacles on the statue?
e: On seeing the reed spectacles, Haldar Sahab shouted, "Stop!" and stood at attention in front of the statue.

q: In what posture did Haldar Sahab stand before the statue when the jeep stopped?
e: In honour of Netaji and the unknown child's patriotism, Haldar Sahab stood strictly at attention before the statue.

q: What is the meaning of the word "Avaak" (अवाक्) in the context of the chapter?
e: "Avaak" means speechless or stunned into silence.

q: In what sense is the word "Kamsin" (कमसिन) used in the chapter?
e: The phrase "masoom aur kamsin" is used for Netaji's statue, meaning youthful and charming.

q: What is meant by "dravit" (द्रवित) at the end of the chapter?
e: "Dravit" means emotionally melted or moved with deep feeling.

q: Which behaviour of the municipality is satirized at the beginning of the chapter?
o: Indecisiveness, bureaucratic delay, and rushing cheap work near the end of its term
e: The story gently satirizes the municipality's bureaucratic delays, low budgets, and hasty last-minute execution of public works.

q: Why did Captain not have a shop of his own?
o: He was a very poor, ordinary street hawker
e: Captain was a poor, old, lame man who earned his living as a street hawker carrying spectacles on a bamboo pole.

q: What kind of person was Haldar Sahab?
e: Haldar Sahab deeply respected patriots and was sensitive enough to recognize and feel moved by Captain's quiet patriotism.

q: What does the word "darkaar" (दरकार) mean in the context of the chapter?
e: In the context of the statue needing spectacles, "darkaar" means need or requirement.

q: What kinds of spectacles did Haldar Sahab see on the statue on his second and third visits?
o: A round wire frame the second time and another new frame the third time
The same thick black frame every time
e: First it was a wide black frame, the second time a round wire-framed one, and the third time yet another frame.

q: Where did the panwala spit his paan while speaking to Haldar Sahab?
o: In the middle of the road
e: The panwala spat his paan below his shop and smiled, showing his red-and-black stained teeth.

q: According to "Netaji ka Chashma", what did Captain do to the statue while changing its spectacles?
o: Cleaned it and asked Netaji for forgiveness
e: The panwala explained that when a customer needed the frame, Captain apologized to Netaji before removing it and placing another.

q: Where in the town was Netaji's statue installed?
o: At the main square of the main market
e: Netaji's marble statue was installed at the main square of the town's main market.

q: According to the narrator, without what did Netaji's statue seem incomplete?
e: Netaji's iconic appearance is tied to both his uniform and his spectacles, so without glasses the statue felt incomplete.

q: Whose name was mentioned on the plaque below the statue in the story?
e: Written beneath the statue was "Sculptor Master Motilal", which revealed to Haldar Sahab that a local teacher had made it.

q: What is the meaning of the word "Kautuk" (कौतुक)?
e: "Kautuk" means wonder, amused curiosity, or pleasant surprise.

q: Upon seeing Captain, what did Haldar Sahab realize about why he was great despite being frail and lame?
o: Because he could run very fast
Because despite physical frailty, genuine patriotism lived in his heart
e: Captain's patriotism rested not on show or physical might, but on sincere feeling and respect.

q: Context: "The town was not very big... a small cement factory, two open-air cinemas, and one (ek tho) municipality too." Why did the author use the colloquial phrase "ek tho"?
o: To bring a natural colloquial regional flavour and mild satire
To make the language heavily Sanskritized
e: "Ek tho" is a colloquial regional expression used by the author to create an authentic small-town flavour with mild irony.

q: Context: "A wide black frame of real spectacles was placed on the statue." Which attitude of Captain toward the statue is revealed here?
o: Affection and deep respect to remedy Netaji's incomplete appearance
e: Captain felt Netaji's statue looked incomplete and hurt without glasses, so he affectionately put real spectacles on it.

q: Context: "Bravo! This idea is great too. The statue is of stone, but the spectacles are real!" What mental state of Haldar Sahab does this reflect?
e: Seeing real spectacles on a stone statue for the first time, Haldar Sahab found the idea unique and commendable, smiling in wonder.

q: Context: "How do Netaji's spectacles keep changing every time?" What trait of Haldar Sahab is evidenced by this question?
e: Noticing the changing frames every fifteen days reflects Haldar Sahab's keen observation and inquisitive nature.

q: Context: The panwala says, "Koi giraak aa gaya samjho..." Which standard word does the colloquial word "giraak" represent?
e: "Giraak" is a colloquial/tadbhav form of "Grahak" (customer), making the panwala's dialogue authentic.

q: Context: "What will that lame man do in the army! He is mad, mad!" Which mindset of a section of society is exposed by the panwala's remark?
o: The insensitive tendency to mock selfless patriotism and label it madness
e: Selfish or insensitive people fail to understand selfless patriotism and dismiss it as madness.

q: Context: "A very old, frail, lame man wearing a Gandhi cap and dark glasses, carrying a small box..." Which literary technique is exemplified here?
e: In just a few words, the author creates a vivid, realistic word-portrait of Captain before the reader's eyes.

q: Context: "For two years Haldar Sahab kept passing through that town and seeing the changing spectacles on Netaji's statue." What does this imply?
o: Haldar Sahab was lazy at work
Captain's patriotism was not a one-day show, but a sustained, living commitment
e: The continuous changing of spectacles over two years proves that Captain's patriotism was enduring and selfless.

q: Context: Saying "Sahab, Captain died," the panwala grew sad and wiped his eyes. What new aspect of the panwala's character emerges here?
o: Beneath his mockery, he too had sensitivity and silent respect for Captain
He was pretending to please Haldar Sahab
e: Though the panwala once called Captain mad, wiping his tears at his death reveals underlying human sensitivity and respect.

q: Context: Haldar Sahab thought, "What will become of a nation that laughs at those who sacrifice (hom dene walon) home, family, youth, and life for their country!" What does "hom dene walon" mean here?
o: Those who sacrifice or dedicate everything
e: The idiom "hom dena" means to offer or sacrifice everything like an oblation in a sacred fire.

q: Context: "Looks for opportunities to sell itself." Which social evil does Haldar Sahab's reflection point toward?
e: Haldar Sahab was pained that society, driven by selfishness and opportunism, mocks patriots instead of valuing them.

q: Context: "Do not stop there today... do not even look at the statue." If Haldar Sahab had strictly kept this resolve, how would the story have ended?
o: The statue would change on its own
He would have missed seeing the reed spectacles and remained in despair
e: Had his eyes not instinctively looked up, Haldar Sahab would have missed the reed spectacles and remained hopeless about the future.

q: Context: "A small spectacle made of reed (sarkanda) was placed on the eyes, just like children make." What does the reed spectacle symbolize?
o: Patriotism and respect for national heroes living on in the new generation (children)
e: The little reed spectacle symbolizes that patriotism is alive and thriving in the younger generation, inspiring hope.

q: Context: Haldar Sahab suddenly shouting "Stop!" from a speeding jeep and standing at attention shows:
o: Deep respect and gratitude for the children's small patriotic gesture
e: Standing at attention is a military salute of honour, showing Haldar Sahab's reverence for the child's innocent patriotism.

q: Contextual analysis: Though the statue at the square was of Netaji, who kept its spirit alive?
o: Captain Chashmewala and finally unknown children
e: The lifeless stone statue was infused with living patriotic warmth by Captain's real spectacles and the children's reed glasses.

q: Context: If Master Motilal had actually carved stone spectacles onto the statue, which central theme of the story would not have emerged?
o: The revelation of ordinary citizens' (Captain's and children's) spontaneous patriotism
e: It was precisely the missing spectacles on the statue that created the space for Captain and the children to express their patriotism.

q: Context: "Why brother? What is the matter? Today there are no spectacles on your Netaji's eyes?" What is the essence of Haldar Sahab saying "your Netaji"?
o: Reminding the panwala that Netaji is the shared heritage and ideal of every citizen
Haldar Sahab did not respect Netaji
e: By saying "your Netaji", Haldar Sahab gently reminds the panwala of his shared bond and civic responsibility toward the leader.

q: Context: "There were spectacles, but not of marble." What contrast does the conjunction "but" highlight here?
o: The contrasting nature of the statue and the spectacles (real glasses on a stone statue)
e: The word "but" highlights the striking contrast between the lifeless marble bust and the real wearable spectacles.

q: Context: "Netaji's statue without spectacles looks bad, rather it hurts him (aahat karti hai)." What feeling does "aahat karna" convey here?
o: Deep emotional pain or hurt to one's feelings
e: "Aahat karna" expresses emotional distress—Captain felt deeply pained seeing his beloved leader without his iconic glasses.

q: Context: Describing the panwala, the author writes, "his belly jiggled (thirkati)." What kind of imagery does this create?
e: The expressive verb "thirkati" creates a vivid, humorous visual image of the panwala's obesity and carefree laughter.

q: Context: If the municipal board's tenure had not been nearing its end, what might have happened?
o: The statue might have been made by a skilled sculptor complete with spectacles
The statue would never be installed
e: It was due to bureaucratic hesitation and the rushing deadline of the ending tenure that the local drawing teacher got the hurried job.

q: Context: In the story, the setting is a small town (qasba)—neither a metropolis nor a tiny village. Why did the author choose this setting?
o: To portray the genuine patriotism of ordinary Indian small-town life
e: Through an ordinary small town, the author shows that patriotism thrives among everyday citizens in every corner of India.

q: Context: "Why brother, what is the matter? How do Netaji's spectacles change every time?" Which tone dominates this dialogue?
e: The exchange between Haldar Sahab and the panwala is natural, friendly, and filled with genuine curiosity.

q: Application: If a reader takes inspiration from Captain's character, what would they adopt in daily life?
o: Serving the country only if recruited into the army
Honouring the nation and its heroes within one's limited means without waiting for high office
e: Captain teaches that even a frail, poor person can practise true patriotism through small, sincere everyday actions.

q: Context: "Master must have made it, but how to make transparent glasses in stone—like real glass—he probably could not decide." What does this sentence express?
e: The phrasing indicates a logical conjecture regarding the technical difficulty the local teacher might have faced.

q: Context: Why was Haldar Sahab initially unsure about whether the spectacle-seller was a patriot or just doing business?
o: Because he was a hawker who even took the frame off the statue for customers, yet replaced it respectfully
e: Giving the statue's frame to a buyer looked practical, yet immediately placing another frame out of reverence proved his true patriotism.

q: Context: What is the exact meaning of the idiom "aankhen bhar aana" used in "Netaji ka Chashma"?
o: Eyes filling with tears out of deep emotion
e: "Aankhen bhar aana" means tears welling up in the eyes due to overwhelming emotion.

q: Context: "The story begins with light humour but ends on a deeply serious and moving note." What does this confirm?
o: The author losing track of the theme
The story's craft of rising emotional depth
e: The narrative progresses skillfully from municipal satire and humour to deep pathos and hope.

q: Application: If a statue of a national hero looks neglected today, what does "Netaji ka Chashma" inspire us to do?
o: Take personal initiative to maintain its cleanliness and dignity
e: The lesson teaches that preserving the dignity of our national icons is every citizen's responsibility, not just the administration's.

q: Context: Haldar Sahab getting off his jeep and standing at attention before the statue highlights which human value?
o: The value of honouring even small noble acts
e: Despite his status, Haldar Sahab honoured an unknown child's tiny reed spectacles with the utmost respect.

q: Through "Netaji ka Chashma", which conventional notion of patriotism does Swayam Prakash challenge?
o: That patriotism is confined only to big leaders, soldiers, or grand ceremonies
That statues should not be built for patriotism
That wearing spectacles is the sole proof of patriotism
e: The author establishes that ordinary citizens—hawkers, children, workers—practice genuine patriotism through quiet everyday acts.

q: In the story, what philosophical contrast does "real spectacles" vs "stone spectacles" symbolize?
o: Living, active human sensitivity vs lifeless, formal tokenism
e: The municipality's statue reflects formal bureaucratic tokenism, whereas Captain's real glasses and children's reed glasses symbolize living empathy.

q: Why is Captain's physical frailty and lameness significant from the perspective of narrative craft?
o: To boost the paan shop's popularity
To show that patriotism springs from inner resolve rather than physical might
e: Juxtaposing the military title "Captain" with a frail body powerfully highlights the triumph of inner spirit over physical strength.

q: Whom does the author satirize by using the phrase "murti banakar patak dene" (making and dumping the statue)?
o: Administrative tokenism and an insensitive, rushed attitude toward public art
e: The verb "patak dena" (dump) exposes bureaucratic indifference—treating a national monument as a mere formality to be disposed of.

q: What kind of thematic resolution does the "reed spectacles" in the final scene leave in the reader's mind?
o: An optimistic, touching ending inspiring faith in the future generation
e: The despair caused by Captain's death transforms into profound hope that the torch of patriotism is safe with the next generation.

q: How are realism and idealism blended in "Netaji ka Chashma"?
o: The entire story is pure fantasy
Administrative apathy and social mockery represent realism, while Captain's and children's quiet devotion represent idealism
It shows only rich people's lives
e: Swayam Prakash weaves lofty ideals of quiet devotion seamlessly within the harsh realism of bureaucracy and social cynicism.

q: What is the narrative role of "Haldar Sahab" in the structure of the story?
o: A silent spectator unrelated to the plot
The sensitive focalizer/observer representing the reader's conscience
e: We experience the town and its characters through Haldar Sahab's observant eyes and conscience; he serves as the story's empathetic focalizer.

q: What kind of realistic small-town character does the author depict through the panwala?
o: An ordinary person who appears mocking and flippant on the surface, yet holds human warmth inside
e: Neither wholly villainous nor idealistic, the panwala mirrors ordinary people who carelessly mock others yet genuinely grieve when they pass.

q: What deeper symbolic meaning does the repeated "changing of spectacles" also suggest?
o: Maintaining a living, evolving connection with national icons across changing times
e: Changing the spectacles prevents the statue from becoming a dead museum piece, keeping it connected to everyday civic life.

q: "What will become of a nation that laughs at those who sacrifice everything for their country"—what tone dominates this line?
o: A sharp tone of introspection and social concern
e: This line is not merely about the panwala; it is a sharp warning and introspection regarding society's moral decline.

q: In the context of the story, how does the theme of "real vs artificial" emerge?
o: The statue is called fake and the panwala real
Artificial glasses are praised over real ones
Real spectacles signify genuine patriotism while the unfinished bureaucratic statue exposes artificial tokenism
Only gold glasses are called real
e: Official formality left the statue incomplete, whereas the common man's real and reed spectacles gave it true completeness.

q: Which characteristic of Swayam Prakash's style makes "Netaji ka Chashma" so readable and impactful?
o: Effortless storytelling, sharp irony, and lively colloquial language
e: His conversational storytelling, sharp irony, and vivid idioms immerse the reader effortlessly without sounding preachy.

q: "A nation is made by all its citizens, rivers, mountains, trees, flora, and fauna"—how does this idea connect to the story?
o: That a nation is built by the love and sense of duty of all its ordinary citizens, not just borders
That statues must be placed on mountains
That glasses should be sold near rivers
e: The essence of the chapter is that the nation thrives through the love and dedication of millions of ordinary citizens like Captain and the children.

q: If the character of the "panwala" were removed from the story, what vital element would be missing?
o: The town's living grapevine, social satire, and the common crowd's mixed mindset
e: The panwala acts as the square's eyes and voice, revealing both Captain's story and society's contradictory attitude.

q: Comparing the two moments—"What will that lame man do in the army!" and "the reed spectacles"—what conclusion emerges?
o: Spectacles should always be made of reed
Children should not join the army
Cynics fade away, while the spirit of selfless patriotism passes from one generation to the next
The panwala asked the children to make it
e: Even after Captain's death, the children's act proves that genuine patriotism is inspiring and endures across generations.

q: Master Motilal's promise to "make and dump the statue in a month" critiques which work culture?
o: Haste, compromise on quality, and a makeshift ("chalta hai") attitude
e: The hurried, makeshift attitude led to compromising quality, leaving a monument of national honour incomplete.

q: Where in Haldar Sahab's character do we see the confluence of "intellectual curiosity" and an "emotional heart"?
o: First he rationally investigates the changing glasses and Captain's name, and at the end tears up seeing the reed glasses
He only asks the driver for directions
He argues over the price of paan
e: Though rational and inquisitive, Haldar Sahab is deeply empathetic, culminating in heartfelt tears at the end.

q: In the story, what two worlds can the "jeep" and the "town (qasba)" be said to connect?
o: The fast-moving modern corporate world and the grounded small-town society
e: Haldar Sahab in his company jeep represents the modern industrial world briefly intersecting with small-town life and values.

q: Captain must have had another real name, yet why did the author not reveal it to the reader?
o: Because the panwala did not know
Because the author forgot his name
Because he represents not one individual, but every unsung ordinary patriot in the country
e: By withholding a personal name, the author elevates Captain into a universal symbol of millions of unsung citizens.

q: The children placing reed spectacles in "Netaji ka Chashma" is the result of what kind of upbringing or value?
o: Spontaneous civic sensibility and the silent influence of Captain's inspiring example
e: Having watched Captain honour Netaji for years, the children absorbed that silent moral lesson and carried it forward.

q: How does "spectacles" in the story rise from an ordinary object to a cultural-national symbol?
o: Because it binds together Netaji's identity, Captain's devotion, and the children's hope
Because everyone could see clearly through it
e: Throughout the narrative, the spectacles transcend mere eyewear to become a symbol of honour, civic duty, and unbroken patriotism.

q: "For the panwala it was an amusing matter, but for Haldar Sahab it was astonishing and deeply moving." What literary insight does this line reveal?
o: The stark contrast between two different levels of social sensitivity toward the same event
e: While superficial observers laugh at Captain's actions, a sensitive observer recognizes the profound patriotism beneath.

q: From the perspective of JAC Board value-based questions, what is the most fitting moral conclusion of "Netaji ka Chashma"?
o: Statues must only be made of bronze
Only wealthy people can be patriots
Every citizen can honour the nation and its symbols through small efforts within their capacity
Paan shops should not exist at intersections
e: The chapter teaches that lack of wealth or physical strength never blocks patriotism; sincere intent is supreme.

q: Why is the English military term "Attention" used just before the concluding line of the story?
o: To show Haldar Sahab knew English well
To accord the unknown child's small gesture an honour equal to a military salute
e: Standing at attention equates the child's humble tribute with a formal military salute of the highest honour.

q: What kind of irony lies in accepting municipal delays while feeling uneasy about a "statue without spectacles"?
o: Emotional and symbolic incompleteness hurts far more than routine civic inefficiency
Spectacles were too expensive in town
e: The missing spectacles felt not just like a flaw in stone, but like a lapse in collective respect.

q: Swayam Prakash's stories highlight middle-class life and the struggles of common people. In "Netaji ka Chashma", which character best embodies this?
o: Captain Chashmewala, who preserves dignity and patriotism amid poverty and frailty
e: Despite poverty, old age, and disability, Captain keeps his human ideals and love for the nation alive.

q: What is the satirical purpose of listing the municipality's miscellaneous acts (roads, urinals, pigeon shelters, poetry meets) at the start?
o: To show special love for pigeons
To prove the municipality is the best in the world
To show that local administration keeps doing random, superficial works without deep planning
To invite readers to a poetry meet
e: Listing odd, disconnected chores before mentioning the statue creates gentle satire on unplanned bureaucratic activity.

q: What similarity existed between Haldar Sahab's and the panwala's final feelings toward Captain?
o: Both ultimately felt Captain's absence and recognized his selfless worth
e: Both the panwala's wet eyes and Haldar Sahab's heavy silence reflect the void left by Captain's passing.

q: As a student reading "Netaji ka Chashma", which element represents the strongest example of symbolism?
o: Real and reed spectacles on the statue—symbolizing living patriotism across generations
e: The changing glasses culminating in the reed spectacles infuse the entire story with rich symbolic meaning.

q: If the story had been titled "Sarkande ka Chashma" instead, how would its impact differ?
o: The climax and final emotional surprise would be spoiled upfront, making "Netaji ka Chashma" a far better title
e: Naming it after the reed spectacles would give away the ending, whereas "Netaji ka Chashma" holds the entire narrative together.
